sources.title: Why we procrastinate
sources.body: Procrastination is often dismissed as simple laziness, but psychologists increasingly view it as a problem of emotional regulation. People tend to delay tasks that make them feel anxious or uncertain, choosing short-term relief over long-term goals. Ironically, the delay usually increases stress, because the task still has to be done in less time. Research suggests that breaking work into small, concrete steps can reduce the anxiety that triggers avoidance. Another useful strategy is self-compassion. Students who forgive themselves for procrastinating on one assignment are less likely to repeat the behaviour next time, perhaps because they spend less energy on guilt and more on the work itself.

sources.title: Rewilding
sources.body: Rewilding is an approach to conservation that aims to restore natural processes rather than manage every detail of a landscape. Instead of planting particular species or controlling grazing by hand, rewilding projects may reintroduce large animals such as beavers or bison and then allow the ecosystem to develop with limited human intervention. Beavers, for example, build dams that slow rivers, create wetlands and reduce the risk of flooding downstream. Critics worry that rewilding can conflict with farming, especially when predators are involved, and that its outcomes are hard to predict. Supporters respond that many traditional conservation methods have failed to halt the decline of wildlife, so a bolder approach is needed.

sources.title: Recycling lithium-ion batteries
sources.body: As electric vehicles become more common, the number of used lithium-ion batteries will rise sharply. These batteries contain valuable materials, including lithium, cobalt and nickel, which are expensive and environmentally damaging to mine. Recycling could reduce the need for new mining, but the process is still developing. Batteries differ widely in design, which makes it difficult to dismantle them automatically. Before recycling, however, many batteries may have a second life. A car battery that can no longer power a vehicle efficiently may still store energy from solar panels for years. Researchers argue that designing batteries to be easily taken apart would make both reuse and recycling far more practical.

sources.title: Polynesian navigation
sources.body: Long before modern instruments, Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean and settled islands across the Pacific, including Aotearoa New Zealand. They relied on detailed knowledge passed down through generations. Navigators memorised the rising and setting points of stars, read the shape and direction of ocean swells, and watched for birds that return to land at dusk. Clouds forming over islands and changes in water colour offered further clues that land was near. In the nineteen seventies, a voyage from Hawaii to Tahiti using only traditional methods helped revive interest in these skills, which are now taught again to new generations of voyagers.

sources.title: Vertical farming
sources.body: Vertical farms grow crops indoors in stacked layers, using artificial lighting and carefully controlled temperature and humidity. Because they do not depend on the weather, they can produce food all year and are often located close to the cities where it will be consumed. They also use far less water than conventional farms, since water is recycled through the system. However, vertical farming has an important limitation: energy. Lighting and climate control are expensive, so most vertical farms grow leafy greens and herbs, which grow quickly and sell for relatively high prices. Staple crops such as wheat and rice are not currently profitable to grow this way. Falling electricity prices from renewable sources could change this calculation.

sources.title: Handwriting and learning
sources.body: As more schoolwork moves onto laptops and tablets, some educators question whether children still need to learn handwriting. Several studies suggest that writing by hand may offer learning benefits. When young children form letters by hand, they appear to recognise those letters more quickly than when they type them. Taking notes by hand may also improve memory of the material, possibly because it is slower and requires learners to summarise ideas rather than copy them word for word. Typing, however, is faster and makes editing easier, which is valuable for longer writing tasks. Many researchers therefore recommend a balanced approach, teaching both skills and choosing the tool that suits the task.

sources.title: Living on a volcanic field
sources.body: Auckland, New Zealand's largest city, is built on a volcanic field that contains more than fifty small volcanoes. Unlike a single large volcano, a volcanic field does not erupt from the same place twice. The next eruption could occur almost anywhere within the field, which makes planning particularly challenging. The most recent eruption formed Rangitoto Island about six hundred years ago. Scientists monitor the region with a network of instruments that detect small earthquakes and ground movement. Because magma rising towards the surface usually produces warning signs, experts expect days or weeks of notice. Emergency planners have therefore prepared evacuation plans that could be adapted to whichever part of the city is affected.

sources.title: The spread of coffee
sources.body: Coffee plants originated in the highlands of Ethiopia, but coffee as a drink first became popular in Yemen, where it was valued by people who needed to stay awake for night-time prayers. From there, coffee houses spread to cities across the Middle East and later to Europe. These coffee houses were more than places to drink. They became important centres of conversation, where merchants exchanged news and customers debated politics. Some rulers viewed them with suspicion and tried to close them. European colonial powers later established coffee plantations in Asia and the Americas, often relying on forced labour. Today coffee is one of the world's most widely traded agricultural products.

sources.title: The value of mangroves
sources.body: Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow in salty coastal water in tropical and warm temperate regions, including northern New Zealand. Their tangled roots trap sediment and slow the movement of water, which helps protect coastlines from erosion and storm damage. Mangrove forests also serve as nurseries for many species of fish, providing shelter for young animals before they move out to sea. In addition, mangrove soils store large amounts of carbon, often more per hectare than many land forests. Despite these benefits, large areas of mangroves have been cleared for fish farms, agriculture and coastal development. Restoration projects have had mixed results, and scientists stress that protecting existing forests is usually cheaper and more effective than replanting.

sources.title: Trials of the four-day week
sources.body: In recent years, companies in several countries have trialled a four-day working week with no reduction in pay. In many of these trials, employees reported lower stress and better work-life balance, and most participating businesses chose to continue the arrangement afterwards. Supporters argue that shorter weeks encourage staff to focus, cut unnecessary meetings and reduce time lost to fatigue. Sceptics point out that the companies that volunteered for trials may have been especially suited to the change, so the results may not apply to every industry. Hospitals, schools and factories, for example, may need to hire additional staff to maintain the same level of service, which would raise costs.

sources.title: Noise and health
sources.body: Noise is often treated as a minor nuisance, but long-term exposure to loud environments can have serious effects on health. Traffic, aircraft and industrial noise have been linked to sleep disturbance, raised blood pressure and a higher risk of heart disease. Even when people believe they have become used to noise, their bodies may continue to react with stress hormones. Children in schools near busy airports have been found to perform worse in reading tests, perhaps because noise interrupts concentration. Cities can reduce the problem through quieter road surfaces, noise barriers and better insulation in homes, as well as by planning housing away from major sources of noise.

sources.title: The unusual platypus
sources.body: When the first platypus specimen reached Britain from Australia in the late eighteenth century, some scientists suspected it was a hoax, made by attaching a duck's bill to the body of another animal. The platypus is indeed unusual. It is a mammal that lays eggs, and males have venomous spurs on their back legs. Its soft bill contains thousands of sensors that detect tiny electrical signals produced by the muscles of its prey, allowing it to hunt with its eyes, ears and nose closed underwater. Platypuses live in rivers and streams in eastern Australia, where they are threatened by drought, dams and land clearing that reduce the quality of their habitat.

sources.title: Open-access publishing
sources.body: Traditionally, academic journals charged libraries expensive subscriptions, so research was available mainly to people at wealthy institutions. The open-access movement argues that publicly funded research should be free for anyone to read. Many journals now publish articles openly, but someone still has to pay for editing and hosting. In one common model, authors or their funders pay a fee when an article is accepted. Critics warn that this can disadvantage researchers from poorer institutions and has encouraged some low-quality journals that accept almost any paper in order to collect fees. Alternative models, such as university-funded journals and public repositories, are attempting to make research accessible without shifting costs onto authors.

sources.title: Where to build wind farms
sources.body: Choosing a location for a wind farm involves balancing many factors. The most obvious is wind speed, because the energy produced rises steeply as wind becomes stronger. Developers also need access to transmission lines, since building new connections to the grid can be very costly. Environmental assessments consider birds and bats, which can be killed by turbine blades, particularly along migration routes. Local communities are another important consideration. Some residents object to the noise and visual impact of turbines, while others welcome payments and jobs. Offshore wind farms avoid some of these conflicts and benefit from stronger, steadier winds, but they are more complex to build and maintain.

sources.title: The psychology of waiting
sources.body: Most of us dislike waiting in queues, but research shows that how long a wait feels can matter as much as how long it actually lasts. Unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, which is why some airports place mirrors or screens near lifts and baggage areas. Uncertainty also makes waiting more stressful; people become calmer when they are told how long the delay will be, even if the news is disappointing. Perceptions of fairness matter too. Customers become especially frustrated if someone who arrived later is served first. For this reason, many banks and offices use a single line that feeds several counters instead of separate lines for each.
